lead: Electric charge is the property that makes two objects push or pull without touching. Coulomb's law gives that push or pull between two point charges: it falls as the square of the distance and points along the line joining them. Every electric field is this law added up over all charges. Engineers use it to find fields near power lines, inside capacitors, and around charged insulators before a circuit is designed.
prereq: You need vector addition from Unit 1 and the gradient and line integrals from Chapter 3.1.

sections.h3: Coulomb's law: force between two point charges

blocks.text: A point charge is a charge whose size is ignored; q₁ and q₂ are its values in coulombs (C), and r is the distance between them in metres (m). The force acts along the line joining the charges. Equal signs repel; opposite signs attract.

blocks.where: F is force in newtons (N); q₁, q₂ are charges in coulombs (C); r is separation in metres (m); ε₀ is the permittivity of free space.

blocks.text: The constant 1/(4πε₀) equals 9×10⁹ N m² C⁻², and ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻². In vector form, the force on charge 1 due to charge 2 is

blocks.where: F₁₂ is the force on charge 1 in N; r̂₁₂ is a unit vector from charge 2 to charge 1; r is the distance between them in m.

blocks.text: Substitute signs directly in the vector form: a negative product flips the force to point from 1 to 2. The magnitude formula removes signs; you then add the direction by hand. Use metres throughout because k is in SI units.
For many charges, compute each pair force and add the results as vectors. This is superposition. Do not add magnitudes unless all forces lie on one line and point the same way.
The electric field E at a point is the force per unit positive test charge placed there:

blocks.where: E is electric field in N/C; F is force on the test charge in N; q₀ is the test charge in C.

blocks.text: For one point charge Q, the field at distance r is

blocks.where: E is field in N/C; Q is source charge in C; r is distance in m; r̂ points radially outward from a positive Q.

blocks.text: The test charge q₀ is imagined small so it does not move the source charges. Once E is known, any charge q at that point feels F = qE.

items: Field lines start on positive charge and end on negative charge.
The tangent to a field line gives the direction of E at that point.
The number of lines through unit area shows the field strength.
Lines never cross, because E has one direction at a point.
For a point charge, lines are radial and evenly spaced in angle.

blocks.text: Symmetric charge distributions are easier with Gauss's law than with direct integration.
An electric dipole is two equal charges +q and −q separated by 2a. Its dipole moment p = q(2a) points from −q to +q.

blocks.where: E(axis) is the field on the dipole axis at distance r from the centre, for r much greater than a; p is dipole moment in C m.
E(equator) is the field on the perpendicular bisector; its direction is opposite to p.

blocks.text: A continuous distribution replaces q by small elements. For a line charge density λ (C/m), surface σ (C/m²), and volume ρ (C/m³), the element charges are dq = λ dl, dq = σ dA, dq = ρ dV.

blocks.where: R is the vector from the element dq to the field point; R is its length; R̂ is its unit vector.

blocks.text: Write the three integrals: E = k ∫ λ dl R̂/R², E = k ∫ σ dA R̂/R², E = k ∫ ρ dV R̂/R². These are vector integrals; in Cartesian coordinates each component is integrated separately.
A point charge is the limit ρ = q δ³(r), where δ³ is the three-dimensional Dirac delta. Symmetric cases are quicker with Gauss's law.

figure.caption: Two charges give a pair force; those forces add as vectors, become an integral for a continuous charge cloud, and are read as a field at each point.

spec.title: From Coulomb to a field
spec.aria: Pair forces are added as vectors, turned into an integral for a continuous distribution, and read as a field at each point.

examples.question: A charge q₁ = +4 μC sits at the origin. A second charge q₂ = −3 μC sits at (0.20 m, 0). Find the force between them and the electric field at the position of q₂ due to q₁. Check that q₂E gives the same force.
steps: List data: q₁ = 4×10⁻⁶ C, q₂ = −3×10⁻⁶ C, r = 0.20 m, k = 9×10⁹ N m² C⁻².
Product q₁q₂ magnitude = 12×10⁻¹² C². Divide by 0.04 m²: 3×10⁻¹⁰. Multiply by 9×10⁹: F = 2.7 N.
Signs are opposite, so the force is attractive. q₂ is pulled toward the origin, that is along −x for q₂.
Field due to q₁ at x = 0.20 m: E = k q₁ / r² = 9×10⁹ × 4×10⁻⁶ / 0.04 = 9×10⁵ N/C. Since q₁ is positive, E points along +x.
Force from field: q₂E = (−3×10⁻⁶ C)(9×10⁵ N/C) = −2.7 N, which is 2.7 N along −x. This matches the direct force.
examples.answer: The force magnitude is 2.7 N, attractive toward the origin; the field due to q₁ at q₂ is 9×10⁵ N/C along +x.
examples.check:
k = 9e9
q1 = 4e-6
q2 = -3e-6
r = 0.20
F = k * abs(q1 * q2) / r**2
E = k * q1 / r**2
F_from_E = q2 * E
print(round(F, 10))
print(round(E, 1))
print(round(F_from_E, 10))

traps: Adding force magnitudes. Two 2 N forces at 60° do not give 4 N; add them as vectors.
Using r in centimetres with k in SI. Convert 20 cm to 0.20 m before squaring.
Reading μC as 10⁻³ C. μ means 10⁻⁶ C; mC is 10⁻³ C.
Forgetting that E due to q₁ at q₂'s position does not include q₂. The field is produced by other charges.
Dropping the sign in vector form and then guessing direction. Either use signs or use magnitude plus a drawn direction.

quiz.q: State Coulomb's law in words and give the value of 1/(4πε₀).
quiz.a: The force between two point charges acts along the line joining them and has magnitude k|q₁q₂|/r², with k = 9×10⁹ N m² C⁻².

quiz.q: Why define electric field as force per unit test charge instead of using force directly?
quiz.a: Dividing by q₀ removes the test charge from the description. E then gives the source's effect per unit charge, and any charge q feels F = qE.

quiz.q: Two charges, 2 μC and 5 μC, are 0.10 m apart in air. Find the force magnitude between them.
quiz.a: F = 9×10⁹ × (2×10⁻⁶ × 5×10⁻⁶) / (0.10)² = 9×10⁹ × 10×10⁻¹² / 0.01 = 9 N. It is repulsive because both charges are positive.

quiz.q: Three equal positive charges sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle. What is the electric field at the centre?
quiz.a: It is zero. Each field has the same magnitude and the three vectors are separated by 120°, so their vector sum is zero. Adding magnitudes would wrongly give three times one field.

quiz.q: Write the field of a point charge Q at distance r. Which way does it point if Q is negative?
quiz.a: E = (1/(4πε₀)) Q/r² r̂, where r̂ points outward from the charge. For negative Q the field points toward the charge.

quiz.q: Find the field at 0.30 m from a 6 μC point charge.
quiz.a: E = 9×10⁹ × 6×10⁻⁶ / (0.30)² = 9×10⁹ × 6×10⁻⁶ / 0.09 = 6×10⁵ N/C, pointing away from the positive charge.

quiz.q: Explain why electric field lines from two charges must not cross.
quiz.a: At any point the electric field has one definite direction. If two field lines crossed, the field at the crossing would have two directions. So field lines cannot cross.

beyond: Not for the exam. Computer tools solve Coulomb superpositions for chips, MEMS sensors and high-voltage insulation by dividing charge into small cells. The method of moments turns the integral equation for a conductor into a matrix. Fast multipole methods and Ewald summation handle millions of charges in molecular simulation. Search for boundary element method electrostatics and fast multipole method to see the same law at industrial scale.
